about: Allele-identity cases. Each pairs a database record of a variant with what a subject's data holds at that position, and gives the outcome: 'match', 'match_after_flip' (the letters fit the record only when complemented, A with T and C with G, and complemented they hold the record's alternate allele), 'ambiguous_strand' (an A/T or C/G site where the letters cannot show the strand and it could change the answer: a homozygous array call, or a data row that gives the record's two letters the other way round), 'ref_alt_swapped' (a data row gives the record's reference as its alternate and its alternate as its reference, as written or after complementing, at a site that is not A/T or C/G) or 'no_match'. Only 'match' lets a pipeline report the record as it stands, so a yes/no matcher should answer yes for 'match' and no for every other outcome. 'no_match' means the data does not confirm the record; it does not mean the person is free of the variant. Array letters may be on either strand of the record's genome build; a data row's reference and alternate are taken as written when its reference agrees with the record's. Coordinates, ids and letters are synthetic and do not describe any real variant or person.

cases.why: The record is a deletion-insertion (AA>C). An array reports two single letters, and A/C fits a plain A>C SNP as well as this record. Two letters cannot tell them apart, so the record must not be reported from this data. It is not ruled out either.

The record is a one-base deletion written with its anchor base, so its alternate allele is the single letter C. A person without the deletion also shows C here. A rule that looks for the alternate letter reports everyone.
The genotype holds G and C. The record's alternate allele is A, so the data shows a different variant at this position.
The data row's own alternate allele is A and the record's is T. Same position, different variant.

T is neither allele of the record. As written, the genotype holds the record's G and a third allele; complemented, it reads C/A and holds no G. The array alone cannot say which, so the record must not be reported, and it is not ruled out.
Both delete bases after the same anchor: one base in the record, two in the data row. Same position, different deletion.

The record and the data row give different reference bases at the same coordinates. Two descriptions that both give the genome's reference bases at a position cannot disagree about them, so one of them is on another build or coordinate system, or is simply wrong. Do not match, and flag the row.

After trimming, both look like the same one-base deletion. But the record's reference is CAA and the data row's is CAT: they disagree about the third base, which trimming throws away. A rule that compares only the trimmed alleles matches them.
An exact single-letter match: one copy of the record's alternate allele, the other copy reference.
Two copies of the record's alternate allele.
The data row's reference and alternate alleles equal the record's, and the genotype holds the alternate.
The same one-base deletion written with a longer anchor (CAA>CA instead of CA>C). Comparing the letters misses it; comparing minimal representations matches it.

T and C are not the record's alleles. Complemented (A with T, C with G) they read A/G: one copy of the record's G. So the letters fit the record only if the data and the record are written on opposite strands. A pipeline may count this only if it corrects strand on purpose, for example from the array manifest, and must not report it as a plain match.

The data row gives T as the reference base where the record gives A. Complemented, the row T>C reads A>G, the record, and the genotype C/C reads G/G: two copies of G. So the row and the record are written on opposite strands, or one of them is wrong. Count it only with deliberate strand correction, never as a plain match.

A and T are each other's complement, so the letters are the same pair on both strands and cannot show which strand the data is on. Here the strand decides the answer: T/T is two copies of T on the record's strand and none on the other. Do not report the record from these letters. Strand information from the array manifest could resolve it; one person's letters and a panel's allele frequencies cannot. This kit uses neither.

C and G are each other's complement, so the letters are the same pair on both strands. C/C is no copy of G on the record's strand and two copies on the other. A rule that complements whenever the letters as written are not a match turns this genotype into a homozygous match. Do not report the record from these letters.

G and C are each other's complement, so the letters are the same pair on both strands and cannot show which strand the data is on. Here that does not change the answer: a heterozygous G/C holds one copy of C on either strand.

The data row gives G as the reference and A as the alternate: the record's alleles the other way round. Two descriptions that both give the genome's reference base at a position cannot disagree about it, so one of them is on another build, lists its alleles in another order (for example effect and other allele), or is wrong. The genotype G/G is two copies of the record's alternate allele, but homozygous reference by the row's own labels. Do not report the record, and check both files.

The record gives A as the reference base and the data row gives T. Complemented, A>T reads T>A, which is also A>T with reference and alternate swapped. So the row may be written on the other strand, where T/T means A/A and no copy of T, or may list the alleles the other way round, where T/T is two copies of T. The letters cannot tell which, so the record cannot be confirmed.

Complemented, C>G reads G>C, which is also C>G with reference and alternate swapped, but here the data row gives C as the reference base, as the record does. The kit takes a data row whose reference agrees with the record as written on the forward strand, as the VCF specification expects (REF is the reference genome's base at POS), so G/G is two copies of G. A row on the other strand with its alleles also swapped would read the same, as can happen in VCFs converted from array data without checking REF against a reference genome; the kit cannot detect it.
